resources.string: Thank you. Your mood can be noted, or we can talk about it. Which first?
A mood can be noted only for today.
Update the earlier mood?
A mood is noted at %1$s: %2$s. Would you like to update it?
A mood was noted at %1$s, a moment ago. Should this one replace it?
Update it
All right, it stays as it is. The next mood can be noted from %1$s.
This one is not saved: the mood noted at %1$s stays.
Here it is as it was noted. Move it to how you feel now, or tap the same word to keep it.
Moods can change through the day. This notes how you feel right now; the next one can be noted from %1$s.
That is good to hear.
Is anything in particular behind it?
What is lifting your mood?
Sometimes a low mood comes without a clear reason.
Good moods do not always need a reason.
Rest or a good sleep
Sport or movement
Something went well
Nature or the weather
Good news
In your words
Would you like to say what it is? It stays in this chat.
Not now
Mood changes
Are these changes very big, and do they go on for a long time or get in the way of everyday life?
If the changes become very big and go on for a long time, or get in the way of everyday life, it is worth talking to a doctor.
Sleep and energy
May I ask two short questions about your sleep and energy these days? You do not have to answer.
Yes, ask
No, thank you
In the last few days, have you noticed any of these?
Needing much less sleep, without feeling tired
Thoughts racing, or hard to concentrate
Doing things unlike me, such as spending a lot or taking risks
Talking much more, or much faster, than usual
Everyday life
Is it getting in the way of everyday life?
If this goes on, it is worth telling a doctor about it, even while you feel good.
Feeling unusually high, or full of energy, while taking %1$s is worth getting advice about today: contact a doctor or an urgent medical helpline.
Thank you, it is noted.
Thank you for sharing it. I hope the day stays this good.
If you would like, we can talk about how you have been feeling.
Talk about how I feel
Put back as it was
updated
NHS, “Bipolar disorder”.
NHS, “Sertraline”, “Fluoxetine”, “Paroxetine”, “Duloxetine” and “Mirtazapine”: serious side effects.
